source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Medium deceptive maze: novelty search (NS) beat objective-based NEAT by about 3x in evaluations. Both solved it in every run.
numbers: NS 18,274 evals (sd 20,447); fitness NEAT 56,334 (sd 48,705); 40 runs each; p<0.001 Student t. Random selection solved only 21 of 40 runs.
limits: Maze is small and the behaviour space is bounded; NEAT neuroevolution, not RL or LLM.
agent_relevance: Searching for new behaviours alone can beat a goal-chasing rule when the goal signal misleads.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Hard deceptive maze: objective search almost never solves it. NS solves it almost every time.
numbers: NS solved 39/40 runs (mean 35,109 evals, sd 30,236); fitness NEAT 3/40; random 4/40.
quote: the same NEAT algorithm can almost never solve it when solving the maze is made the explicit objective
limits: Maze built to be deceptive by the authors.
agent_relevance: Strongest 'abandon the objective' result. Hints that when the agent is stuck, a novelty pull can beat a goal pull.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Biped walking: NS gaits went further than fitness-based gaits, and fitness search often fell into a bad local optimum.
numbers: 50 runs: NS 4.04 m (sd 2.57) vs fitness 2.88 m (sd 1.04) in 15 s, p<0.01; best NS gait 13.7 m; more than 40% of fitness runs stuck in non-oscillatory gaits.
limits: Simulated biped, one task.
agent_relevance: Second domain with the same pattern; the effect is not maze-only.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Boundary condition: NS fails when behaviour space is unbounded. Fitness also fails there, so NS is not worse.
numbers: Unenclosed maze, 100 runs: NS solved 5, fitness NEAT solved 2 (not significantly different).
quote: constraining the space of possible behaviors is important in some domains for novelty search to be efficient
limits: Authors' own test; shows NS needs a bounded space.
agent_relevance: Open mode needs bounds on what counts as new, or novelty drifts into trivial variation.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning objectives: evolution through the search for novelty alone
finding: Boundary condition: how behaviour is described matters. A coarse behaviour grid slows NS, and using fitness as the behaviour measure removes most of the gain.
numbers: Hard maze: grid size 4x4 (16 behaviours) took 117,107 evals, about 3x slower than original, still better than fitness; 4 of 960 runs needed a restart. Fitness as behaviour: 11/40 solved vs fitness NEAT 4/40 (p<0.05 Fisher). Archive limited to population size 250 still solved 40/40, 38,324 evals, not significantly different.
limits: Authors' own ablations, same maze.
agent_relevance: Novelty must be measured on a descriptor that is not the goal score. For the agent: define novelty on answer approach, not on answer score.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011) Critical factors in the performance of novelty search
finding: Independent analysis of why NS works. Performance depends on the behaviour function: dropping irrelevant behaviour features helps a lot, grouping behaviours with different downstream potential hurts a lot.
numbers: Artificial grid, 70 runs, cap 2e6 evals: with 3 irrelevant behaviour points 21/70 runs failed, with 4 points 29/70 failed. Removing symmetry cut mean cost from 63,440 to 27,427. Wrongly aliased version found the optimum in only 6/70 runs.
limits: Mostly artificial domain plus three deceptive mazes (NEAT). Descendant fitness probability is only computable in toy domains.
agent_relevance: The choice of what counts as different is the main lever. Irrelevant dimensions waste the search budget.

source: Kistemaker & Whiteson (2011) Critical factors in the performance of novelty search
finding: Merging behaviours helps only if the merged ones have similar future potential. Over-merging turns NS into random search.
numbers: Supercell grouping: performance dropped suddenly when cell size exceeded the mutation range (cell 2 to 5 for mutation +-3; 5 to 10 for +-6; 10 to 20 for +-12).
limits: Artificial domain; some wall-grid differences were not significant because of high variance.
agent_relevance: Too coarse a novelty descriptor removes the signal. Keep the descriptor fine enough to separate approaches.

source: Gomes, Urbano & Christensen (2013) Evolution of swarm robotics systems with novelty search
finding: Independent robotics replication in swarm robots: NS bootstraps evolution and is unaffected by deception, but the authors note earlier work found it does not beat fitness on non-deceptive tasks.
numbers: Fitness-based evolution: 10/30 runs near max fitness, 10/30 found no viable solution. Random evolution fitness below 0.2.
quote: Previous studies have shown that novelty search can perform better than fitness-based evolution in deceptive tasks
limits: Simulation only, two swarm tasks; hybrid NS plus fitness variants did better than pure NS.
agent_relevance: Pure novelty is weaker than novelty plus goal pressure when the goal is not deceptive. Mixed mode is safer.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: MAP-Elites (grid of niches, keep best per niche) beat traditional EA, novelty search with local competition and random sampling on quality-diversity measures.
numbers: Retina problem, 20 replicates: MAP-Elites higher on global performance, reliability, precision and coverage at p<1e-7. Soft robot task: significantly higher reliability and coverage (p<0.002); global performance not significantly different (p>0.05); worse precision (p<0.01).
limits: Simulated tasks; worse precision because it spreads evaluations over many cells.
agent_relevance: Keeping the best answer per approach-niche gives variety without losing the best answer. A cheap archive design for open mode.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: Stepping stones: elites often descend from a good neighbour a medium distance away, so a diverse archive feeds later good solutions.
numbers: Lineages of four random elites crossed many map regions; no sampled organism had a parent more than halfway across the map.
limits: Descriptive analysis of lineages.
agent_relevance: Keep failed or odd partial ideas as seeds; they may lead to a good answer elsewhere.

source: Tao, Francois-Lavet & Pineau (2020) Novelty search in representational space for sample efficient exploration
finding: Novelty (k-nearest-neighbour distance) in a learned low-dimensional space gave sample-efficient exploration in deterministic mazes and Acrobot, compared with count, prediction error, RND and Bootstrapped DQN.
numbers: 5 trials per setting. Normalised combined steps to goal: random 3.26 (SE 0.41, p=3.1e-5) vs this method 1.00. Multi-step maze: random 1863 steps, RND 1669, BDQN 525. Table columns are garbled in extracted text, so other rows are not reliable.
limits: Deterministic environments only; 5 trials; Welch t-tests, small N. Authors exclude stochastic baselines.
agent_relevance: Novelty must be measured in a space that drops irrelevant detail. For text, compare ideas by meaning, not by wording.

source: Tao, Francois-Lavet & Pineau (2020) Novelty search in representational space for sample efficient exploration
finding: The novelty score is the same sparseness formula as Lehman & Stanley (average distance to k nearest), and the paper shows it is inversely related to pseudo-count visit probability.
numbers: Theorem 1: score goes to 0 as the whole state space is visited.
quote: This is also the same score used to gauge 'sparseness' in behavior space in Lehman and Stanley (2011).
limits: Theory for finite communicating MDPs.
agent_relevance: Links novelty search to count-based exploration. Novelty fades once the space is covered, so open mode needs a stopping rule.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019/2021) Go-Explore: a new approach for hard-exploration problems
finding: Go-Explore: archive of visited states, return to a promising one, then explore. It broke hard-exploration Atari games where intrinsic-motivation agents scored near zero.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: mean 43,763 without domain knowledge, 666,474 with it (best run over 18 million, 1,441 levels). Pitfall: mean 59,494, max 107,363; earlier methods scored 0. Phase 1 without domain knowledge reached mean 57,439; level 1 after mean 640M frames.
limits: Relies on a resettable or deterministic simulator in training; authors state results assume deterministic training is allowed.
agent_relevance: Explicit memory of promising partial states plus returning to them beats a novelty bonus alone. Matches a branch-and-resume search design.

source: Taiga et al. (2020) On bonus based exploration methods in the Arcade Learning Environment
finding: Re-test under one common setup found recent exploration bonuses do not beat plain epsilon-greedy much, and hurt on easy games.
numbers: Rainbow agent, 200M frames, seven hard-exploration games plus the Atari training set. Pseudo-count was worse on every training-set game except Seaquest; RND and ICM only matched epsilon-greedy.
quote: bonus-based methods are generally detrimental in the context of easy exploration problems
limits: Atari only; fixed learning algorithm; Montezuma gains not significant in their setting.
agent_relevance: Exploration bonuses have a cost when the problem is easy. Switch novelty on only at an impasse.

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through large models
finding: Evolution through Large Models: a code LLM as the mutation operator inside a quality-diversity search (MAP-Elites) filled most of a 1,728-niche map from one seed, and fine-tuning on accepted diffs raised the share of valid diffs.
numbers: 1,728 niches; runs averaged over 3 seeds per seed program; nearly all seeds filled the map, the Square seed slowly. Models trained on the 80% quality threshold dataset (95K examples) did better than the 50% threshold (280K).
limits: Sodarace walkers only; speed of niche filling varies by seed.
agent_relevance: An LLM can supply meaningful variation, which random mutation cannot. Diversity can be bootstrapped from one example.

source: Bradley et al. (2023) Quality-diversity through AI feedback
finding: QDAIF: LLM judges both quality and which niche a text falls in. It beat non-QD baselines on QD score in all domains, and human ratings partly agree with the AI judge.
numbers: Human study (mean over opinions, story genre, story ending): human QD score QDAIF 0.772 vs Fixed-Few-Shot 0.767, Shuffling 0.696, Random-Search 0.606, LMX-quality-only 0.650. Human-AI agreement 0.833 vs human-human 0.800. Fixed-Few-Shot had higher mean quality rating (4.13 vs 3.90). 5 seeds.
quote: The correlation drops when the evaluated quality is in the range 0.995 to 1
limits: Authors suspect reward hacking of the LLM judge at the top of the quality range; small human study by authors and colleagues; the human QD edge over Fixed-Few-Shot is tiny.
agent_relevance: LLM-judged niches work, but the judge can be gamed near the top. Use a second check on top-scoring ideas.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) OMNI: open-endedness via models of human notions of interestingness
finding: OMNI: an LLM picks which learnable tasks are also interesting. It beat learning-progress-only and uniform curricula, and came close to a human-made oracle of interestingness.
numbers: Crafter: LP alone learned 55 tasks (9 interesting), OMNI 82 tasks (14 interesting); success on interesting tasks 0.52 (LP) vs 0.78 (OMNI). Differences p<1e-3 Mann-Whitney. OMNI vs oracle mostly not significant (p>0.05). BabyAI: 4 vs 8 tasks learned.
limits: Two grid-world domains; the oracle was built by the authors; LP is distracted by boring but learnable tasks.
agent_relevance: A language model can stand in for 'worth exploring'. Judging interest, not just novelty, avoids wasting steps on trivial variants.

source: Faldor et al. (2025) OMNI-EPIC: open-endedness via models of human notions of interestingness with environments programmed in code
finding: OMNI-EPIC extends OMNI with an archive of tasks, including failed ones, and environments written as code. Human users partly agreed with its success detector.
numbers: One run: 16 tasks learned, 6 failed, 1 judged uninteresting. User study with 50 participants: 72.7% alignment between human evaluation and the success detector.
limits: Alignment only 72.7%, so the automatic success check disagrees with people about a quarter of the time; single illustrative run.
agent_relevance: Failed attempts are useful stepping stones. Keep a failure log in the open-mode archive; verify the automatic success check.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming: open-ended generation of diverse adversarial prompts
finding: Rainbow Teaming: quality-diversity search over adversarial prompts reached very high attack success and beat baselines without stepping stones.
numbers: 2000 iterations, archive of 100 prompts: about 92% attack success on Llama 2/3 chat, 98% on Mistral 7B and Vicuna 7B (GPT-4 judge). About 50% of prompts transfer to other models, up to 66% on GPT-4o. Fine-tuning on the data cut ASR from 92%/95% to 0.3%/0.7%. Human-human agreement 83% vs human-GPT-4 81%, Llama Guard 78%.
limits: Judge is an LLM; ablation baselines were no stepping stones and same-cell mutation, both worse.
agent_relevance: Using archived neighbours as parents (stepping stones) mattered. Diverse search finds many failure cases; useful for self-testing answers.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Voyager: an LLM agent with an automatic exploration curriculum, a skill library and self-checking beat other LLM agents in Minecraft.
numbers: 160 prompting iterations, 3 trials: 63 unique items (3.3x more), 2.3x longer travel, wooden tool 15.3x faster, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x; only agent to reach diamond (1 of 3 runs, 102 iterations). ReAct and Reflexion reached none. Random curriculum cut items found by 93%.
quote: The discovered item count drops by 93% if the curriculum is replaced with a random one
limits: Three trials per method; baselines were adapted from text tasks; GPT-4 cost.
agent_relevance: Order of exploration matters: an adaptive curriculum beats random order by a large margin. A skill library stops the plateau.

source: Lu et al. (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore
finding: Intelligent Go-Explore replaces hand-made novelty rules with a foundation model that judges what is interesting. It beat LLM agents such as ReAct and Reflexion on search-style tasks.
numbers: Game of 24: 100% success, 70.8% faster than the next best baseline (depth-first search). BabyAI 'put next to': statistically significant 36% gain over second best (chi-square, p<0.05); 25 seeds. TextWorld Coin Collector: only method to find long optimal paths.
limits: Mostly text or small grid tasks; gap grows with task difficulty; cost of many model calls.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct LLM test of 'archive plus return plus model-judged interest'. Fits open mode with branch and resume.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: evaluating language models for humanlike diversity
finding: LLMs lack output diversity. Larger models in a family are often less diverse. Asking for creativity helps little; regenerating in context with prior outputs in view helps most.
numbers: 20 models, 10 samples at temperature 1. Frontier models produce on average fewer than 3 distinct answers in 10 queries, and utility under 4 of 10; Gemma 2-2B and Llama 3.2-1B were most diverse. In-context regeneration roughly matched human writers; GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceeded their utility. Paraphrasing and system prompts only marginally helped.
limits: Human baseline is 8 author-written answers per prompt, a homogeneous group, so a lower bound on human diversity.
agent_relevance: Direct support for a scaffold that shows earlier attempts and forces a different approach. Plain resampling gives near-copies.

source: Hughes et al. (2024) Open-endedness is essential for artificial superhuman intelligence
finding: Position paper: defines open-endedness as a system that produces artifacts both novel and learnable to an observer, and argues foundation models plus open-ended search are the path to superhuman AI.
numbers: No new experiments; formal definition based on novelty and learnability.
limits: Opinion and framing paper, no measured result; also covers safety risks.
agent_relevance: Gives a usable definition for the open mode: keep only outputs that are new and also learnable or useful to the user.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: Ablation: without the skill library, the agent matched Voyager early but plateaued late and never reached diamond. A hand-made curriculum did worse than the automatic one.
numbers: Tech tree iterations (3 trials): Voyager wooden 6 +-2, stone 11 +-2, iron 21 +-7, diamond 102 (1/3). Without skill library: 7 +-2, 9 +-4, 29 +-11, diamond N/A (0/3). AutoGPT: wooden 92 +-72, iron 135 +-103, diamond 0/3.
limits: Three trials; diamond reached once; high variance.
agent_relevance: Stored reusable results keep late-stage progress going. Open mode should save what it learned, not just wander.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2019/2021) Go-Explore: a new approach for hard-exploration problems
finding: Authors name two failure modes of novelty-driven agents: detachment (forgetting promising areas) and derailment (exploring from a state without first getting back to it). Go-Explore fixes both with an archive and a return step.
numbers: Before Go-Explore, best intrinsic-motivation agents scored 2,500 or lower on Montezuma's Revenge in stochastic tests and 0 on Pitfall.
limits: Authors' own hypothesis for why earlier methods fail; tested on two Atari games.
agent_relevance: Two named risks for open mode: dropping a good lead (detachment) and branching from a half-remembered state (derailment). Log leads and restore state before branching.
